questions.q: A detective wants to catch a killer before the next full moon; underneath, she can't let anyone help her. Which is the want and which the need?
choices: Both are needs: one outer, one inner
The want is to accept help; the need is to catch the killer
The want is to catch the killer; the need is to let others help
Neither: she has a super-objective, not a want
questions.explain: The want is the conscious, outward goal; the need is the inner change she doesn't yet see.

questions.q: At the end of Casablanca, Rick puts Ilsa on the plane with her husband. In want-and-need terms, what has happened?
choices: He gives up his want for his need
He finally gets his want
He has a flat arc and changes no one
His wound is revealed
questions.explain: He sacrifices what he wanted (Ilsa) for what he needed (to rejoin the world and its fight).

questions.q: A writer's draft opens with a ten-minute flashback showing exactly how the hero's mother abandoned him, and the hero later explains it to a friend. What would Truby advise?
choices: Keep it: the audience must know the wound first
Turn the flashback into the inciting incident
Reveal the ghost later, when the audience already cares, and less completely
Cut the friend and keep the flashback
questions.explain: Truby suggests revealing the ghost late; critics of the trauma plot would add: don't let it explain everything.

questions.q: The hero of a long-running detective series never changes; instead, each case tests her beliefs and changes the people around her. What is this?
choices: A negative arc
Static conflict
A jumping arc
A flat arc
questions.explain: K. M. Weiland's flat arc: the protagonist already holds the truth, and the story tests it.

questions.q: What was Parul Sehgal's main complaint in "The Case Against the Trauma Plot"?
choices: Trauma is never a fit subject for fiction
Trauma has become a default shortcut to depth that reduces characters to symptoms
Writers don't research trauma accurately enough
Trauma plots are always too slow
questions.explain: She argued the withheld-then-revealed wound had become a formula that flattens people.

choices: Super-objective: Truby; ghost: Stanislavski
Bone structure: McKee; dramatic need: Egri
Super-objective: Stanislavski; bone structure: Egri
The Lie: Field; ghost: Weiland
questions.explain: Stanislavski's super-objective is the actor's version of the want; Egri's bone structure is physiology, sociology, psychology.

questions.q: A reporter writing about a released prisoner decides he 'needed to forgive himself' and builds the piece toward that. What's the problem?
choices: The need is the writer's interpretation, imposed on a real person
Features shouldn't have structure
The want should come after the need
Nothing, if it makes a good kicker
questions.explain: Wants can be reported in the subject's own words; a 'need' or an arc imposed from outside turns a person into a character.

questions.q: In Citizen Kane, how does the film treat the 'Rosebud' explanation?
choices: It reveals the wound as the full answer to Kane
It never shows what Rosebud is
It reveals the sled but has the reporter doubt that one word can explain a life
It explains Rosebud through a psychiatrist's speech
questions.explain: The film offers the wound and refuses to let it be the whole answer. The psychiatrist's speech is Psycho.

ideas: Which approach sets a character's conscious goal against the inner change they don't know they must make?
Which approach traces a character's present weakness back to a single injury in their past?
Which approach warns that a withheld-then-revealed trauma has become fiction's shortcut to depth?
Which approach describes a hero who doesn't change but changes the world around them?
